vignette:
Elena was 38, a community organizer in a bustling neighborhood of Chicago, and she had spent most of her life trying to outrun a childhood she could barely hold in her mind. The traumatic event was not a single moment but a climate, a season of years: her father's rages, the way his hand would close around her small arm, the feeling of being pinned against a wall in her own bedroom with no way out. She remembered fragments with startling clarity-the pattern of the wallpaper, the sound of his belt buckle hitting the floor-but other stretches were blank, as if her mind had simply erased them. Sometimes, when she tried to recall what happened, she felt nothing at all, just a hollow numbness, as though the girl in those memories was a stranger.

Now, as an adult, those fragments returned without warning. A memory of the event would come to mind suddenly-not as a story, but as a picture, a vivid image of a doorway or a shadow-and it would leave her feeling trapped, as if she had no options. That feeling of entrapment was the worst part, because it made her uncomfortable in her own skin, and it was this discomfort that drove her to act. When the memory surfaced, she would throw herself into work or tasks to keep her mind occupied, staying late at the office until her eyes burned. She tried to erase the memory of the event entirely, telling herself it didn't happen, but the images kept coming. The discomfort also made her scan every room she entered for a seat with her back against a wall, so she could see the whole space. She had come to believe that if she could not see everyone, someone could corner her again.

The memories themselves fed her sense of danger. The clearer the image-the wallpaper, the buckle-the more she felt the need to check behind her when she walked down the street, certain that someone was following her. And the more she checked, the more she noticed shadows and sounds that seemed to confirm the threat. This vigilance made it hard to fall asleep because she needed to stay alert, and the exhaustion only made the memories more intrusive, as if her tired mind had fewer defenses. She was caught in a loop: the memory triggered the threat, and the threat triggered more memory.

Elena's negative appraisals of herself deepened the cycle. She felt dead inside, hollowed out, and she was certain that she was a weak person because she hadn't stopped the abuse. Somebody else, she thought, would have fought back or run away. These beliefs made her push herself harder at work, overcommitting to projects to prove she was strong, and they made her choose her seat before anyone else could, because she was sure that if she didn't protect herself, no one else would. The numbness also colored her memories: when she recalled the event without emotion, she took it as proof that she was broken, which only reinforced her belief that she was weak.

The strategies she used to cope made things worse. Sitting with her back to the wall meant she could never relax, and the constant vigilance kept her memories close to the surface, ready to spring. Overworking left her exhausted, and in that exhaustion, the intrusive images came more frequently. Erasing the memory was impossible, and trying to do so only made her more aware of its presence. She had stopped going to community meetings in certain buildings because she couldn't find a seat that felt safe, and her partner had started to worry about her distance at night, when she lay rigid in bed, listening for footsteps.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was a moment at a neighborhood rally, when a colleague touched her shoulder from behind. She had spun around, heart pounding, and seen the confusion on the woman's face. She was afraid of what she might become-someone who could not do her job, someone who could not be touched. She wanted to stop feeling trapped in a past she could barely remember, and she was terrified that she never would.
